in_text_mentions: In the acute stage, the margins of the patellar tendon become blurred in radiographs due to the soft tissue swelling. After three to four months, bone fragmentation at the tibial tuberosity is viewed. In the sub-acute stage, soft tissue swelling resolves, but the bone ossicle remains. In the chronic stage, the bone fragment may fuse with the tibial tuberosity which can appear normal. However, sometimes the bone fragment is displaced (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial MRI showing a large, free ossicle and related pathology in the context of Osgood-Schlatter disease. B: Sagittal T1-weighted MRI demonstrating the separation and location of the ossicle in the infrapatellar fat pad. C: Sagittal T2-weighted MRI showing active inflammation and bone marrow edema, indicating active Osgood-Schlatter disease. D: Coronal MRI revealing small, separated ossicles inferior to the main bony prominence.
panels.attribution_text: Choi and Jung. Intra-articular Large Ossicle Associated to Osgood-Schlatter Disease.. Cureus 2018. doi:10.7759/cureus.3008. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Right knee magnetic resonance images. (A) A large ossicle with heterogenous signal intensity (arrow) and a Baker’s cyst (asterisk) are seen on axial image. (B) From T1-weighted sagittal image, the ossicle (arrow) is separately located inside the infrapatellar fat pad. (C) T2-weighted sagittal image shows inflammation of patellar tendon (solid arrow) and bone marrow edematous change of anterior tibia plateau (dotted arrow). (D) Small separated ossicle (arrow) was found inferior to the large ossicle from coronal image.
in_text_mentions: Right knee magnetic resonance images showed about 3.8 x 1.3 x 3.0 cm sized, well-circumscribed ossicle. Several smaller ossicles were also found near the tibial tubercle. Inflammatory changes in synovium, infrapatellar fat pad, and patellar tendon were also seen. A reactive bone marrow edema was found at the anterior aspect of the tibial condyle. Besides, a Baker’s cyst of 7.3 x 4.1 x 14.7 cm size was found (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A is a lateral plain radiograph of the right knee showing an isolated osseous lesion (arrow) at the infrapatellar area, consistent with Osgood-Schlatter disease. B: Panel B is a lateral plain radiograph of the left knee showing an osseous body partially fused to a hypertrophied tibial tuberosity, consistent with Osgood-Schlatter disease.

in_text_mentions: Plain radiographic examination of the right knee showed a large ossicle locating beneath the patellar tendon and inside the infrapatellar fat pad. A similar-sized ossicle was seen in the left knee, while it was partially fused to the hypertrophied tibial tuberosity (Figure 1).

plate_findings.evidence: Conventional radiography of the knee showed fragmentation of the tibial tuberositas pointing towards Osgood Schlatter Disease (Figure 1A).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Lateral X-ray of the knee (Panel A) clearly demonstrates fragmentation of the tibial tuberosity, which is a direct finding for Osgood-Schlatter disease. B: High frequency ultrasound (Panel B) shows imaging findings of hypoechoic tendon and increased power doppler signal compatible with Osgood-Schlatter disease. C: Ultrasound (Panel C) shows an anechoic structure identified as a patellar ganglion cyst, which is diagnosed as possibly related to coexisting chronic Osgood-Schlatter disease.
panels.attribution_text: Mebis et al. Intratendinous Patellar Ganglion Cyst with Coexistant Osgood Schlatter Disease.. Journal of the Belgian Society of Radiology 2016. doi:10.5334/jbr-btr.1195. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: (A) Lateral X-ray of the knee; (B & C) High frequency ultrasound of the patellar tendon, sagittal plane.
in_text_mentions: A 19-year-old boy was sent in by the general practitioner with complaints of persisting tenderness and swelling just below the knee. Conventional radiography of the knee showed fragmentation of the tibial tuberositas pointing towards Osgood Schlatter Disease (Figure 1A).

a high frequency linear probe was performed. Findings included fragmentation of the tibial tuberosity, hypoechoic tendon and increased power doppler signal, compatible with Osgood Schlatter disease (Figure 1B). Additionally, a sharply delineated, elongated anechoic structure with enhanced through transmission occupied the center of the patellar tendon (Figure 1C). A small pedicle towards the proximal bony fragment of the tibial tuberosity seemed to be present. The diagnosis of an intratendinous patellar ganglion cyst was made, possibly related to a coexistant chronic Osgood-Schlatter disease.
